Thirty-four comments

This tune starts off with same first phrase as “The Sally Gardens” which can be quite confusing. It’s probably not a good idea to play both tunes in one set.

The first part starts and ends with a fairly long G which could be nicely ornamented with a roll.

Apart from that, the tune is fairly straightforward and a lot of fun to play, especially as part of a set of fast reels at sessions. Try following this tune with a good, fast reel in D.

↳ Posted by Jeremy on June 2nd, 2001.

In our sessions we have found this tune goes well with The Scholar.
The origin of the word “teetotaler” apparently goes back to a British parliamentary debate in the 19th century when the subject of abstinence (from alcohol) was being discussed. One of the speakers was advocating total abstinence, but, because he had a slight speech impediment it came out as “t-total abstinence”. Hence the word “teetotal”.

trevor

↳ Posted by fidicen on December 3rd, 2002.

I find the bit about the speech impediment highly unlikely, Trevor. Stuff like anecdotal accounts and acronyms used to explain the origin of words almost always get made up after the event and then become fact just because people repeat what they heard from someone else. The “T-” is more likely just for emphasis.

↳ Posted by Dr. Dow on August 21st, 2005.

Found this on the internet, so it MUST be true…

“There is general agreement that the first use of ”teetotal" in reference to abstention from alcohol was in a speech to an English temperance society by a man named Richard Turner in 1833. Whereas some of his contemporaries drew a moral distinction between beer and hard liquor, Turner urged his listeners to abstain totally from all alcohol.

Contrary to popular legend, there is no evidence that Turner recommended “tea” as an alternative to alcohol, or that his listeners were urged to mark the letter “T” for “Total Abstinence” on their pledge cards at the meeting. The “tee” tacked onto the front of “total” was just a common way, at that time, of giving extra emphasis to a word, a process linguists call “reduplication.” (And yes, the term “reduplication” has always struck me as weirdly redundant.) The use of “teetotal” to mean “absolutely, totally” is well-documented in other, non-alcoholic writings of the day. For instance, one author, writing in 1885, had occasion to write, “I hope I may be tee-totally ruinated, if I’d take eight hundred dollars for him.” "

↳ Posted by Schy on September 13th, 2005.

The Teetotaller-acronyms and Irish tune names.

I agree with Dow: acronymic origins of words are suspect and unlikely. Take the Australian example of the common name for an emigrant from the Mother Country: POMMIE. It is often asserted that the derivation is from convict days:Prisoner Of Mother England. Unlikely, in my opinion. If one considers the complexion and “funny” accent of the “New Chum” then much more appealing is the idea that the childish chant and sarcastic association of: “Immigrant….Pomegranate!; Immigrant….Pomegranate!”, (despite the disparity of syllables) is much more likely. Pomegranates, the fruit with the red,rosy sunburnt appearance, grow well in the antipodes. The names of Irish tunes are most likely to be based on the simplest origins. It is food for thought in another posting that there is a wonderful lack of religiosity in Irish tune names. Apart from the occasional Father Whosit’s Fancy the music remains secular.

Re: The Teetotaller’s

Learned this song about 50 year ago with these lyrics. Can anyone possibly tell me where it originally came from? Apologies if I didn’t get all the verses written correctly. My recollection is that a band from Boston played it when visiting with some of us in Oregon, but I don’t remember who was in the band! Any revisions would be gladly considered. I usually played the fiddle tune in the key of G, but could only sing this acapella in the key of D.

TEMPERANCE REEL
(remembered by David Altman as played by a group from Boston in the 1970s; also called The Teetotaller’s)

The other day I got an invitation to a funeral,
But to my disappointment the fella didn’t die!
He said that he was sorry for havin’ disappointed us,
And seein’ as he apologized, we let the thing go by.

For to ease our disappointment he took us out and treated us
And bought a quart of porter for a company of ten.
Then when someone asked him whose money he was squanderin’
The fella took out his wallet and we didn’t ask again.

Well we bought a concertina for to kick up all rascalities,
And none of us could play it though we tried our best and worst.
We made an awful noise with it and played the thing
So carefully til’ all the bellows burst.

We bought a boiled potato for to mend the concertina with
When someone hit Maloney with a carcass of a cat.
He bundled up his whiskers and then read out the riot act.
He swore he’d put 2 heads upon the bugger that done that.

The owner of the beer shop saw us all a-riotin’
And gave orders to get out but to that we all refused.
So he whistled in some loafers who were standin’ on the corner
And for 10 or 15 minutes we were bodily abused.

When we left the beer shop down the road we started
And a bunch of hungry urchins pelted us with mud.
We told them all to chuck it and they said they were doin’ it
And then they all run off and left us where we stood.

The next thing we met was a group of Salvationers.
They riffled all our pockets and asked us, “Were we saved?”
Poor little John McGinty got escorted to the station house
For askin’ a big policeman if his appetite was shaved.

For to free McGinty we all took off our undershirts
And down to the pawn shop marched the bloomin’ lot.
We told them we only wanted 10 and 6 on them.
“There’s enough already on ‘em!” was the answer that we got.

We got the 10 and 6 for all to free McGinty with.
Bad luck to the beer shop we passed along the way!
We couldn’t pass up to take some refresherments
And we squandered every penny of the fine we had to pay!

The drink being in us, sure all the sense was out of us,
And for a bit of riotin’ we quickly did repair.
We battered one another til’ we were worth 3 ha’pence.
You could have carpeted the floor with all the skin and hair.

Well, McGinty hit McGinty, and McGinty hit some other man,
And every man hit every man against whom he held a spite.
Poor crippled McNamara (who was sittin’ sayin’ nothin’)
Got a kick that broke his jaw for not indulgin’ in the fight.

We fought away like Turks til’ the police separated us.
They took us to the prison with broken noses and black eyes.
I got 60 days in prison and for me it was a lesson.
I’LL GO NO MORE TO FUNERALS UNTIL THE FELLA DIES!
